items.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

Checkpoint What it is Defaults
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein Time step distilled, for fast inference 16 steps, no CFG
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base Base model 50 steps, CFG

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

TL;DR

  • One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control.
  • The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100.
  • NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with from_single_file, for smaller GPUs.
  • LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing.
  • Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own.

Contents

  • Getting started
  • What FLUX.3 can do
  • Base model and quantized variants
  • LoRA finetuning
  • What it costs to run
  • The architecture
  • Modular Diffusers
  • Try it

Getting started

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

pip install -U diffusers transformers

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein")
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.to("cuda")

pipe(prompt="a red fox", output="images")[0].save("fox.png")

What FLUX.3 can do

Text-to-image

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

prompt = (
    "A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. "
    "The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath "
    "visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes "
    "across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows."
)

fox = pipe(
    prompt=prompt,
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output="images"
)[0]
fox.save("fox.png")
Text to image

Image-to-image

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

prompt = (
    "The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue "
    "moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light."
)
night = pipe(
    prompt=prompt,
    image=fox, # from the previous text to image example
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output="images",
)[0]
night.save("night.png")
Image to image

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as <ref_image_0>, <ref_image_1>, ... in the order they are passed to image:

red_fox = pipe(prompt="a red fox", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
bench = pipe(prompt="a wooden bench", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]

combined = pipe(
    prompt="The fox from <ref_image_0> sitting on the wooden bench from <ref_image_1> in a snowy setting.",
    image=[red_fox, bench],
    output="images",
)[0]

combined.save("combined.png")
<ref_image_0>: a red fox <ref_image_1>: a wooden bench The fox on the bench

Layout control

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as <id>.

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Placing regions in a new image 

layout_prompt = (
    "Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person <silhouette_1> centered against a "
    "solid, vibrant chartreuse background <background_1>. The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running "
    "pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. "
    '[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle '
    'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A '
    "black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing "
    'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]'
)

runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
Each region's desc is drawn inside its bbox

Moving regions within a reference image

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

from diffusers.utils import load_image

knight_image = load_image("knight_orig.png")
edit_prompt = (
    "In <ref_image_0>, move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure <knight_1> upwards and to the left along the "
    "yarn cliff <cliff_1>. Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop "
    "<backdrop_1>, the large knitted dragon <dragon_1>, and the fiery orange thread <fire_1>. "
    '[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], '
    '"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], '
    '"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], '
    '"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, '
    '{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], '
    '"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, '
    '{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], '
    '"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], '
    '"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]'
)

moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
The knight moves from its src_bbox to its tgt_bbox, and the rest of the scene stays put

Base model and quantized variants

Base model

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base")
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")

pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale=5.0)  # optional
image = pipe(prompt=prompt, output="images")[0]

Single-file format checkpoints

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

from diffusers import BFLQuantizationConfig, Flux3Transformer2DModel, ModularPipeline

model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"
variant = "fp8r"  # or "nvfp4"

transformer = Flux3Transformer2DModel.from_single_file(
    f"https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/variants/{variant}/model.safetensors",
    config=model_id,
    subfolder="transformer",
    quantization_config=BFLQuantizationConfig(compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16),
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.update_components(transformer=transformer)
pipe.to("cuda")

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

Variant Fast kernels on Other GPUs
fp8r Compute capability 8.9+ (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell) Weights are dequantized each step: lower memory, no speedup
nvfp4 Blackwell, with flashinfer-python and flashinfer-cubin at the same version Same as above

LoRA finetuning

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein.py \
  --pretrained_model_name_or_path="black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" \
  --dataset_name="multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain" \
  --caption_column="caption" \
  --instance_prompt="trtcrd" \
  --output_dir="trained-flux3-tarot-lora" \
  --mixed_precision="bf16" \
  --resolution=1024 \
  --use_aspect_ratio_buckets \
  --train_batch_size=1 \
  --rank=16 \
  --lora_alpha=16 \
  --learning_rate=1e-4 \
  --lr_scheduler="constant" \
  --max_train_steps=1500 \
  --validation_prompt="a trtcrd of a cat, tarot style" \
  --validation_epochs=25 \
  --seed=0 \
  --push_to_hub

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

  --gradient_checkpointing \
  --cache_latents \
  --use_8bit_adam

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as <ref_image_0>.

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

What it costs to run

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

Memory

name peak allocated (after load) GiBs peak allocated (after inference) GiBs
nvfp4 (RTX6000) 13.4 15.3
fp8r (H100) 14.35 16.27
bf16 (H100) 18.80 20.72

If you have less memory:

  • Load a quantized transformer.
  • Run the text encoder separately and free it. It only runs once per image, before denoising (see Encode once, generate many).
  • Turn on automatic CPU offloading, which moves each component to the GPU only while it runs (we didn't benchmark this)
from diffusers import ComponentsManager, ModularPipeline

manager = ComponentsManager()
manager.enable_auto_cpu_offload(device="cuda")

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein", components_manager=manager)
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
# no pipe.to("cuda"): the manager handles device placement

Speed

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Workflow Output size Time Peak memory
Text-to-image 1024 × 1024 1.93 s 23.8 GiB
Image-to-image, one 1024 × 1024 reference 1024 × 1024 3.87 s 23.8 GiB
Layout editing (the knight), one 1360 × 768 reference 1360 × 768 4.10 s 23.8 GiB

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Stacked bars of tokens per transformer call: text-to-image 4,256 tokens; image-to-image 8,272; layout text-to-image 4,336; layout image-to-image 8,800

The architecture

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

  1. text
  2. the noisy image being generated
  3. and optional reference images

From pixels to tokens

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

From prompt to tokens

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

Two stages

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

  1. Stage 1: per-mode blocks. Each stream goes through 5 blocks with its own weights. Text has its own blocks, the noisy image has its own, and the reference images have their own.
  2. Stage 2: joint blocks. The streams are concatenated into one sequence, [text | image | reference], which goes through 28 blocks that share one set of weights.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Inside one block

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

def block(x, shift, scale, gate):      # shift, scale, gate come from the token's timestep embedding
    h = layer_norm(x)                  # no learned scale or shift
    h = (1 + scale) * h + shift
    q, k, v = to_q(h), to_k(h), to_v(h)
    q, k = rope(rms_norm(q)), rope(rms_norm(k))
    out = attention(q, k, v) + mlp(h)  # parallel, MLP is SwiGLU
    return x + gate * out

Every token gets its own timestep

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Positions in four dimensions

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Tokens t: timestep h: height w: width l: length of sequence
text token i 0 0 0 i
image token at (row, col) 0 row / 2 col / 2 0
reference k at (row, col) 0 row / 2 col / 2 −(k + 1)

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

The denoising loop

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

Step 1 Step 5 Step 10 Step 15 Step 25 Step 50

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

Modular Diffusers

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

See the workflows

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

from diffusers import Flux3AutoBlocks

blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks()
print(blocks.available_workflows)
# ['text2image', 'image_conditioned']

print(list(blocks.get_workflow("text2image").sub_blocks))
# ['text_encoder', 'denoise.input', 'denoise.prepare_latents', 'denoise.set_timesteps',
#  'denoise.prepare_rope_inputs', 'denoise.denoise', 'denoise.after_denoise', 'decode']

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Encode once, generate many

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline

model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"

blocks = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id).blocks
text_blocks = blocks.sub_blocks.pop("text_encoder")  # `blocks` now starts at the VAE encoder

text_pipe = text_blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)
text_pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
text_pipe.to("cuda")

state = text_pipe(prompt=prompt, negative_prompt="")  # no guider here, so ask for the negative embeddings

prompt_embeds = state.get("prompt_embeds")
negative_prompt_embeds = state.get("negative_prompt_embeds")

del text_pipe
torch.cuda.empty_cache()

image_pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)  # no text encoder to load
image_pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
image_pipe.to("cuda")

for seed in range(3):
    image = image_pipe(
        prompt_embeds=prompt_embeds,
        negative_prompt_embeds=negative_prompt_embeds,
        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed),
        output="images",
    )[0]
    image.save(f"{seed}.png")

Add a step inside the loop

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

from diffusers.modular_pipelines import Flux3AutoBlocks, InputParam, ModularPipelineBlocks, OutputParam


class Flux3PreviewStep(ModularPipelineBlocks):
    model_name = "flux3"

    @property
    def inputs(self):
        return [InputParam("latents"), InputParam("noise_pred")]

    @property
    def intermediate_outputs(self):
        return [OutputParam("x0_previews", type_hint=list)]

    @torch.no_grad()
    def __call__(self, components, block_state, i, t):
        if i == 0:
            block_state.x0_previews = []
        sigma = t / 1000  # timesteps are sigmas scaled to [0, 1000]
        block_state.x0_previews.append(block_state.latents - sigma * block_state.noise_pred)  # x0 = x_t - sigma * v
        return components, block_state


blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks()
denoise_loop = blocks.sub_blocks["denoise"].sub_blocks["text2image"].sub_blocks["denoise"]
denoise_loop.sub_blocks.insert("preview", Flux3PreviewStep(), 1)  # between "denoiser" and "after_denoiser"

pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")

out = pipe(prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output=["x0_previews", "images"])

Try it

  • Fine-tune: DreamBooth LoRA scripts
  • Prompting: Black Forest Labs prompting guide

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

Checkpoint
What it is
Defaults



black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein
Time step distilled, for fast inference
16 steps, no CFG


black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base
Base model
50 steps, CFG





You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!




TL;DR



One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control.
The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100.
NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with from_single_file, for smaller GPUs.
LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing.
Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own.




Contents



Getting started
What FLUX.3 can do

LoRA finetuning
What it costs to run
The architecture
Modular Diffusers
Try it




Getting started


Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):
pip install -U diffusers transformers

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:
import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein")
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.to("cuda")

pipe(prompt="a red fox", output="images")[0].save("fox.png")





What FLUX.3 can do








Text-to-image


FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.
prompt = (
    "A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. "
    "The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath "
    "visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes "
    "across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows."
)

fox = pipe(
    prompt=prompt,
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output="images"
)[0]
fox.save("fox.png")






Text to image










Image-to-image


Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.
prompt = (
    "The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue "
    "moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light."
)
night = pipe(
    prompt=prompt,
    image=fox, # from the previous text to image example
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output="images",
)[0]
night.save("night.png")






Image to image




With several references, refer to them in the prompt as <ref_image_0>, <ref_image_1>, ... in the order they are passed to image:
red_fox = pipe(prompt="a red fox", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
bench = pipe(prompt="a wooden bench", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]

combined = pipe(
    prompt="The fox from <ref_image_0> sitting on the wooden bench from <ref_image_1> in a snowy setting.",
    image=[red_fox, bench],
    output="images",
)[0]

combined.save("combined.png")








<ref_image_0>: a red fox
<ref_image_1>: a wooden bench
The fox on the bench










Layout control


Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as <id>.
Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.




Placing regions in a new image


layout_prompt = (
    "Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person <silhouette_1> centered against a "
    "solid, vibrant chartreuse background <background_1>. The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running "
    "pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. "
    '[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle '
    'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A '
    "black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing "
    'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]'
)

runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]






Each region's desc is drawn inside its bbox










Moving regions within a reference image


For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.
This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:
from diffusers.utils import load_image

knight_image = load_image("knight_orig.png")
edit_prompt = (
    "In <ref_image_0>, move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure <knight_1> upwards and to the left along the "
    "yarn cliff <cliff_1>. Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop "
    "<backdrop_1>, the large knitted dragon <dragon_1>, and the fiery orange thread <fire_1>. "
    '[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], '
    '"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], '
    '"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], '
    '"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, '
    '{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], '
    '"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, '
    '{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], '
    '"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], '
    '"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]'
)

moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]






The knight moves from its src_bbox to its tgt_bbox, and the rest of the scene stays put










Base model and quantized variants








Base model


Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).
pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base")
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")

pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale=5.0)  # optional
image = pipe(prompt=prompt, output="images")[0]





Single-file format checkpoints


Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.
from diffusers import BFLQuantizationConfig, Flux3Transformer2DModel, ModularPipeline

model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"
variant = "fp8r"  # or "nvfp4"

transformer = Flux3Transformer2DModel.from_single_file(
    f"https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/variants/{variant}/model.safetensors",
    config=model_id,
    subfolder="transformer",
    quantization_config=BFLQuantizationConfig(compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16),
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.update_components(transformer=transformer)
pipe.to("cuda")

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

Variant

LoRA finetuning


FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).
Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:
accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein.py \
  --pretrained_model_name_or_path="black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" \
  --dataset_name="multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain" \
  --caption_column="caption" \
  --instance_prompt="trtcrd" \
  --output_dir="trained-flux3-tarot-lora" \
  --mixed_precision="bf16" \
  --resolution=1024 \
  --use_aspect_ratio_buckets \
  --train_batch_size=1 \
  --rank=16 \
  --lora_alpha=16 \
  --learning_rate=1e-4 \
  --lr_scheduler="constant" \
  --max_train_steps=1500 \
  --validation_prompt="a trtcrd of a cat, tarot style" \
  --validation_epochs=25 \
  --seed=0 \
  --push_to_hub

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:
  --gradient_checkpointing \
  --cache_latents \
  --use_8bit_adam

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.
A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as <ref_image_0>.
See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

def block(x, shift, scale, gate):      # shift, scale, gate come from the token's timestep embedding
    h = layer_norm(x)                  # no learned scale or shift
    h = (1 + scale) * h + shift
    q, k, v = to_q(h), to_k(h), to_v(h)

    out = attention(q, k, v) + mlp(h)  # parallel, MLP is SwiGLU
    return x + gate * out





Every token gets its own timestep


In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.
The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.
The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.




Positions in four dimensions


Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Tokens
t: timestep
h: height
w: width
l: length of sequence



text token i
0
0
0
i


image token at (row, col)
0
row / 2
col / 2
0


reference k at (row, col)
0
row / 2
col / 2
−(k + 1)




Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.




The denoising loop


FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.
At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:










Step 1
Step 5
Step 10
Step 15
Step 25
Step 50




The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.
If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.




Modular Diffusers


FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.




See the workflows


You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.
from diffusers import Flux3AutoBlocks

blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks()
print(blocks.available_workflows)
# ['text2image', 'image_conditioned']

print(list(blocks.get_workflow("text2image").sub_blocks))
# ['text_encoder', 'denoise.input', 'denoise.prepare_latents', 'denoise.set_timesteps',
#  'denoise.prepare_rope_inputs', 'denoise.denoise', 'denoise.after_denoise', 'decode']

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.




Encode once, generate many


Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.
import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline

model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"

blocks = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id).blocks
text_blocks = blocks.sub_blocks.pop("text_encoder")  # `blocks` now starts at the VAE encoder

text_pipe = text_blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)
text_pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
text_pipe.to("cuda")

state = text_pipe(prompt=prompt, negative_prompt="")  # no guider here, so ask for the negative embeddings

prompt_embeds = state.get("prompt_embeds")
negative_prompt_embeds = state.get("negative_prompt_embeds")

del text_pipe
torch.cuda.empty_cache()

image_pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)  # no text encoder to load
image_pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
image_pipe.to("cuda")

for seed in range(3):
    image = image_pipe(
        prompt_embeds=prompt_embeds,
        negative_prompt_embeds=negative_prompt_embeds,
        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed),
        output="images",
    )[0]
    image.save(f"{seed}.png")





Add a step inside the loop


The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:
from diffusers.modular_pipelines import Flux3AutoBlocks, InputParam, ModularPipelineBlocks, OutputParam


class Flux3PreviewStep(ModularPipelineBlocks):
    model_name = "flux3"

    @property
    def inputs(self):
        return [InputParam("latents"), InputParam("noise_pred")]

    @property
    def intermediate_outputs(self):
        return [OutputParam("x0_previews", type_hint=list)]

    @torch.no_grad()
    def __call__(self, components, block_state, i, t):
        if i == 0:
            block_state.x0_previews = []
        sigma = t / 1000  # timesteps are sigmas scaled to [0, 1000]
        block_state.x0_previews.append(block_state.latents - sigma * block_state.noise_pred)  # x0 = x_t - sigma * v
        return components, block_state


blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks()
denoise_loop = blocks.sub_blocks["denoise"].sub_blocks["text2image"].sub_blocks["denoise"]
denoise_loop.sub_blocks.insert("preview", Flux3PreviewStep(), 1)  # between "denoiser" and "after_denoiser"

pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")

out = pipe(prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output=["x0_previews", "images"])





Try it

items.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.content:
🤗 Models | 📄 Paper | 📓 Tutorial notebooks | 🌎 Demo

We introduce HiRO-ACEv2, the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.

HiRO-ACE, introduced earlier in 2026, has two parts: ACE, an AI model that operates at a coarser 100 km resolution, and HiRO, a model that sharpens those coarse outputs into fine 3 km detail. The biggest change in HiRO-ACEv2 is the new downscaling model, HiROv2, which can now 1) predict several high-resolution fields at once instead of just rainfall, so it can capture a much wider range of extreme weather, and 2) has improved skill in predicting extreme events.

Our main focus with HiRO-ACEv2 was to simulate extreme events well. Changes to how we train HiROv2 improved its ability to reproduce the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values. When given coarsened X-SHiELD data, it matches the target simulation's high-resolution statistics to within 3%, even for events so rare they occur only once in a million data points. It also accurately estimates the total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms it never saw during training, and generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands, though winds and pressure around the eye remain somewhat more lopsided than in X-SHiELD. Additionally, HiROv2 realistically generates strong winds flowing down mountain slopes.

We also trained an updated version of ACE for this system. Over a 10-year simulation, its hurricanes, average climate patterns, and overall distributions of rain, wind, and pressure all line up well with X-SHiELD. That tells us ACE's coarse simulations are a solid foundation for producing long-term high-resolution climate data.

Putting HiROv2 and ACE together, we generated a full year of global 3 km data. Its statistics closely match X-SHiELD's, even though HiRO was working from a simulation ACE ran on its own rather than from real X-SHiELD data. Across a 10-year run, the energy of HiRO-ACEv2's hurricanes is comparable to X-SHiELD's over the same period, and snapshots from that run show a variety of other extreme events that resemble those in X-SHiELD.

An example of a strong hurricane in the North Atlantic, generated during the 10-year HiRO-ACEv2 simulation.

Overall, HiRO-ACEv2 offers researchers a flexible and inexpensive way to generate many versions of high-resolution rain, wind, and pressure data for extreme events over 10 years or more. Producing global high-resolution data with it costs roughly 300 times less than running X-SHiELD. If only one region is needed, the savings can be more than a hundred times greater, depending on the size of the area. We're also working on a streamlined version of HiROv2 that could make it more than ten times faster still.

We still have future work ahead of us: because HiRO learned from X-SHiELD, it only works with the version of ACE tuned to match X-SHiELD. That means it can't yet produce high-resolution data for other climates, such as a warmer future or the historical record in datasets like ERA5. Next, we plan to train on new X-SHiELD datasets, including one simulating a world 4°C warmer, so the system can handle different climates. We also plan to add outputs like near-surface temperature and snow and ice, which would allow for even more uses, such as snowpack prediction.

Visualizing and using HiRO outputs

Simulated 10 m wind speed over Baja California in the ACE data visualizer: ACE2 at 100 km resolution on the main map and HiRO-ACEv2 at 3 km in the inset.

A simulated storm over the northeastern Pacific in the ACE data visualizer. The main map shows 10 m wind speed at 100 km resolution; the 3 km HiRO-ACEv2 inset shows finer structure within the storm.

To make it easy to see what HiRO produces without running any inference, we built a web demo that shows pre-generated precipitation, wind, and sea-level pressure output from HiROv1 and HiROv2 side by side with X-SHiELD, the simulation they were trained on. The demo complements the quantitative comparisons in our tech report: it offers a quick visual check of how the outputs look, and lets users zoom in on their own region of interest to judge performance there.

For more in-depth analysis, the models are available to download, and our tutorial notebooks walk through how to run them.

items.title: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
items.content:
LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

  • Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19.
  • Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap.
  • Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

  1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
  2. Teacher specialization
  3. Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks.
  4. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks.
  5. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.

Benchmark results

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B)
AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61
BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78
ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13
LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72
PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20
τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01
WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69
GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42
AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58
HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65
IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19
IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67
Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34
MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40
SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40
SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Inference speed on CPU and GPU

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

pip install -U transformers

Then load and run the model:

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="auto",
    dtype="bfloat16",
#   attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True)

prompt = "What is C. elegans?"

input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    tokenize=True,
)["input_ids"].to(model.device)

output = model.generate(
    input_ids,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.05,
    max_new_tokens=512,
    streamer=streamer,
)

Use it in your agent harness

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

hermes config set model.provider custom
hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1
hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B
hermes config set model.context_length 131072
hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions
hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

  • Download: LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base and LFM2.5-24B-A2B on Hugging Face.
  • Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi.
  • Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Citation

If you use this work, please cite the release blog:

@article{liquidAI202624BA2B,
  author  = {Liquid AI},
  title   = {LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents},
  journal = {Liquid AI Blog},
  year    = {2026},
  note    = {www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b},
}

Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19.  
Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap.  
Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.





How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters


LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.
Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)  
Teacher specialization  
Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks.  
MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks.  
Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.





Benchmark results


We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.




Inference speed on CPU and GPU


LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B


Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.
Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Then load and run the model:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="auto",
    dtype="bfloat16",

)

streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True)

    [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    tokenize=True,
)["input_ids"].to(model.device)

    input_ids,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.05,
    max_new_tokens=512,
    streamer=streamer,
)





Use it in your agent harness


Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:
hermes config set model.provider custom
hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1

hermes config set model.context_length 131072
hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions
hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.




Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B


Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:
Download: LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base and LFM2.5-24B-A2B on Hugging Face.

items.title: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

How I prompt ML Intern

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

1. A model that knows your field

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

2. A model that draws your character

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

3. A model that does a new trick

  1. Camera-angle LoRAs are among the most-liked community add-ons for earlier Qwen-Image models. You can give the model a picture of an object and ask to see it 45 degrees from the left. When I checked a few days after the Qwen-Image 2.1 model release, nobody had made one, so I tasked ML-intern to build it.

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

  1. Doodle-in LoRA is another cool idea. Upload a photo with a magenta scribble on it and add a short prompt naming an object. The LoRA replaces the scribble with that object while keeping the original lighting and composition consistent.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

4. A model that fits your device

  1. The Pocket Rewriter from the top of this post is the first one. ML-intern started by generating 8,797 short image requests with a small instruct model through Inference Providers, following a mix set in my prompt: photos, posters, logos, infographics and more, about a third of them asking for exact text in quotes, and many in languages other than English. The 9B teacher then rewrote all of them on one A100 in 2 hours 37 minutes (~USD 6.50). After filtering for quality, 1,840 examples were selected for training dataset.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

  1. Agate-Preview-002-4step is the second. Logolabs' Agate Preview 002 is a 260M-parameter text-to-image model, small enough for a browser, but it needs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 network passes per image. I asked ML-intern to distill it down to just 4 passes!

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

What it cost

Model Base model Compute
Citrus Doctor Qwen3.5-2B USD 1.90
Huggy LoRA FLUX.2 klein base 4B USD 7.60
Pocket rewriter (0.8B and 2B) Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B USD 16.05
Viewpoint Orbit LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 16
Doodle-in LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 24.30
Agate 4-step (two runs) Agate Preview 002 USD 37
Total about USD 103

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

Make yours

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. summaries.en: I needed a smaller, CPU-compatible prompt rewriter for Qwen-Image 2.1, as the official 9B model was memory-intensive. I used ML Intern, an AI agent, to create a 0.8B version that runs on CPU, returning valid output 99.7% of the time and using less compute. I described my requirements to ML Intern, which planned, budgeted, and executed the task, costing $16 for the entire project. Over several days, I created five more models using this method, each starting as a prompt in HuggingChat and ending as a public model on Hugging Face with evaluations. My prompts, ranging from 450 to 2,000 words, detailed the model's purpose, dataset, base model, and training script, including verified facts to avoid redundant work. Key prompts included baseline evaluations and smoke tests to ensure value before full training. I capped costs at $12 per project, requiring ML Intern's permission for exceeding the budget.

items.title: Introducing Falcon ASR
items.content:
English · العربية

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Try Falcon ASR →

Recognising spoken Arabic

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

Arabic benchmark results

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Evaluating Emirati speech

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

Training for different recording conditions

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

English and other languages

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Model foundation

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Try Falcon ASR

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

Acknowledgments

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

جرّبوا Falcon ASR ←

التعرف على العربية المنطوقة

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

نتائج الاختبارات العربية

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تقييم اللهجة الإماراتية

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

التدريب على ظروف تسجيل مختلفة

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

الإنجليزية واللغات الأخرى

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

أساس النموذج

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

تجربة Falcon ASR

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

شكر وتقدير

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.
أساس النموذج
يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.
تجربة Falcon ASR
يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.
شكر وتقدير
نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.
كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

summaries.en: Falcon ASR is a 1.6B parameter Arabic speech recognition model developed at TII Abu Dhabi, with a focus on Emirati dialect. It also supports English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese. Evaluations show an average WER of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets (best published result 23.17%) and the lowest WER/CER among compared systems for Emirati speech (WER 22.73%). The model handles dialects, background noise, overlapping speech, and multiple languages using shared weights. Public demos and API access are planned.
